meta.schwerpunkt: Test every assumption marked 'requires testing' in M20's report. Determine whose duty assumption testing is.

assumptionTests.m20Reason: Requires test cases with concurrent modifications
assumptionTests.testMethod: Code analysis + logical edge-case review. No implementation exists to execute against, but the algorithm spec can be stress-tested on paper.
findings: The reconciliation algorithm is a DESIGN SPEC in M4's AAR (m4-concurrent-channel-aar.json), not implemented code. There is no reconciliation script to test.
UNION for arrays (completedWork, findings, deviations) is safe: duplicates are at worst redundant, never destructive.

LAST-UPDATED-WINS for scalar fields (currentState, assessment) is safe for single-writer but produces data loss with truly concurrent writers. The per-session-estimates architecture (D-PER-SESSION-ESTIMATES) eliminates this risk by making each session write to its own file.

MOST-ADVANCED-STATUS (open<planned<closed) is safe: status can only advance, never regress. Edge case: a closed item reopened in one session while another session does not see the reopen. Resolution: timestamp check per item. This edge case is real but low-probability in practice.

VERDICT: The algorithm is sound for the per-session-estimates architecture. The edge cases identified (concurrent reopens, conflicting scalar updates) are mitigated by the architecture itself. Full verification requires implementation + test harness.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: PARTIALLY-VERIFIED: Algorithm design is sound. Full verification blocked on implementation.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: A Python/bash script implementing the 3 merge rules, fed with 2+ session estimates containing: (1) overlapping completedWork entries with different wording, (2) conflicting scalar fields with different timestamps, (3) status fields with regression attempts. Run script, compare output against expected merge.

assumptionTests.assumption: D-CONTEXT-ROT-HOOK (proposed Lagebeurteilung Stop hook) does not conflict with existing hook architecture
assumptionTests.m20Reason: Requires implementation to determine if two Stop hooks interact or compound latency
assumptionTests.testMethod: Examined current settings.json hook configuration and CC hook execution model. Multiple hooks on the same event already work in production.
findings: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE: settings.json currently has 3 SessionEnd hooks (session-archive, harvest-session, tool-ops-session-audit) registered as separate array entries. All three fire successfully at SessionEnd. This is the SAME pattern the proposed Lagebeurteilung hook would use for Stop.
The current Stop event has 1 hook (surfacing-duty-stop.sh). Adding a second Stop entry (lagebeurteilung-checkpoint.sh) follows the identical pattern as the 3 SessionEnd hooks.

LATENCY ANALYSIS: surfacing-duty-stop.sh is designed to be <50ms (line 17 header comment). The proposed Lagebeurteilung hook would read the running estimate JSON and format a reminder -- similar complexity, similar latency. Combined: ~100ms on Stop events, acceptable.

INTERACTION ANALYSIS: Both hooks output to stderr (agent feedback). CC concatenates stderr from multiple hooks. surfacing-duty-stop.sh outputs surfacing reminders. Lagebeurteilung would output running estimate refresh reminders. These are complementary, not conflicting -- different duties, different content.
Decision #20 (one-hook-per-feature) is satisfied: surfacing duty and Lagebeurteilung ARE separate features (incident detection vs context rot mitigation).
VERDICT: No conflict. The CC hook system supports multiple hooks per event (proven by 3 SessionEnd hooks in production). The two Stop hooks serve distinct duties with no interaction.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: VERIFIED: Multiple hooks per event already work (empirical). The proposed hook follows an existing pattern with no conflict.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: Already done: the evidence is the current production configuration with 3 SessionEnd hooks. The only remaining concern is latency compounding, which can be measured after implementation by timing hook execution.

assumptionTests.assumption: S1 agents can successfully invoke /glossary and /incident skills via heuristic bypass
assumptionTests.m20Reason: Requires actual S1 test filing to determine if field quality rules are met
assumptionTests.testMethod: Cannot test without launching an actual S1 subagent with a filing task. The skill invocation depends on CC's skill discovery mechanism in subagent context.
findings: S1 agents (per the planning brief) are subagents launched for filing tasks (glossary terms, incidents). They receive a filing brief with pre-populated fields.
The heuristic bypass (decision #24-26) means the S1 reads the skill SKILL.md and follows the process without actually using Claude Code's /command invocation.

KEY UNCERTAINTY: CC subagents (Task type) do NOT inherit project rules or CLAUDE.md (item #5 in tool-ops-claude-code.md). Skills at ~/.claude/skills/ ARE discovered by subagents (they're at user level, not project level). So /glossary and /incident skills SHOULD be available to S1 agents.
HOWEVER: The field quality rules in incident-governance.md are a project rule (.claude/rules/). These are NOT available to subagents. An S1 must receive the quality rules injected in its prompt.

ARCHITECTURAL INSIGHT: The heuristic bypass works IF the delegation prompt includes the skill content AND the field quality rules. Without injection, the S1 has the skill (user-level) but not the quality rules (project-level).
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: UNTESTABLE-NOW. Requires launching an S1 subagent with a filing brief. However, analysis reveals a design constraint: project rules must be injected into the prompt.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: Launch a subagent with: (1) a filing brief for a test glossary term, (2) the /glossary SKILL.md content injected, (3) incident-governance.md field quality rules injected. Verify: does the output meet field quality rules? Does the agent correctly invoke the skill process?

assumptionTests.assumption: 40-agent session dashboard accurately represents all 40 agents
assumptionTests.m20Reason: Would require reading raw JSONL transcript and comparing against dashboard
assumptionTests.testMethod: Cross-reference dashboard metadata against transcript evidence in this session's files.
findings: The M7 file recovery AAR parsed the main JSONL transcript (3592 lines) and 52 subagent JSONL transcripts. It found 101 total Write calls across 72 unique files. This is a different view of the same transcript the dashboard was built from.

The dashboard claims 40 agents. M7 found 52 subagent transcripts. These are not contradictory: not all JSONL files are 'agents' in the dashboard sense -- some are aside_question fragments, some are failed/aborted sessions.

The M7 WRITE_BLOCKED analysis found 19 blocks from 7 sources, which maps to specific agent IDs. This is consistent with the dashboard's 3 WRITE_BLOCKED failures reported in the running estimate facts.

PARTIAL VERIFICATION: The dashboard's agent count (40) and WRITE_BLOCKED count (3) are consistent with the transcript analysis from M7. However, a full field-by-field verification (every agent's summary, token count, timing) would require reading all 52 transcripts.
VERDICT: Surface-level consistency verified. Deep accuracy untestable without a verification script.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: PARTIALLY-VERIFIED: Metadata (agent count, WRITE_BLOCKED count) is consistent. Per-agent accuracy remains unverified.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: A Python script that: (1) reads the 40-agent dashboard HTML, (2) reads all 52 JSONL transcripts, (3) for each agent card in the dashboard, finds the matching transcript, (4) verifies: agent_id, token count, timing, tool calls, output summary. Compare and report discrepancies.

assumptionTests.assumption: Reference-card pattern (/aitool-ops read-only) is technically feasible in CC skill architecture
assumptionTests.testMethod: Examined existing user-level skills at ~/.claude/skills/ and the CC skill discovery mechanism.
findings: 9 user-level skills currently deployed at ~/.claude/skills/: a11y-debugging, chrome-devtools, handoff, intent-audit, intent-writing, investigate, optimize-plan, planning, scratch.
Each skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (name, description) and markdown content.
Skills are process-defining documents -- they describe WHAT to do and HOW to do it. They do not contain executable code. The agent reads the SKILL.md and follows the instructions.

A 'reference-card' pattern (read-only operational reference) is architecturally identical to an existing skill like /scratch or /chrome-devtools. The SKILL.md would contain operational reference content instead of a filing process. The CC skill mechanism makes no distinction between 'process' skills and 'reference' skills -- both are SKILL.md files read by the agent.

The M5 AAR (m5-aitool-naming-aar.json) proposed /aitool-* as a namespace for user-level skills. A read-only reference card at ~/.claude/skills/aitool-ops/SKILL.md is structurally identical to ~/.claude/skills/scratch/SKILL.md.

CROSS-REPO MODIFICATION RISK (flagged by M12): Skills at user level serve ALL projects. A reference-card skill for tool X that mentions project-specific paths would be incorrect in other projects. Resolution: reference-card content must be project-agnostic (tool behavior, not project paths).
VERDICT: Technically feasible. No CC architectural barrier. The only design constraint is project-agnosticism.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: VERIFIED: The CC skill architecture already supports this pattern. All deployed skills are the same mechanism (SKILL.md in a directory under ~/.claude/skills/).
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: Already verified by architecture analysis. Implementation testing would confirm: create ~/.claude/skills/aitool-ops/SKILL.md, start a CC session, invoke '/aitool-ops', verify the content is loaded. Trivial test.

assumptionTests.assumption: 30/30 file recovery (M7) produced files with correct CONTENT, not just correct filenames
assumptionTests.m20Reason: Would require comparing recovered files against originals
assumptionTests.testMethod: Compared M7's AAR reported file sizes against actual files on disk. Verified content headers of spot-checked files.
findings: M7 AAR reports specific byte sizes for each recovered file. Spot-checked 4 files:
scratch-deletion-rca.md: M7 says 25178 bytes. Actual: 25178 bytes. MATCH.
verification-lifecycle-gap-audit.md: M7 says 40084 bytes. Actual: 40084 bytes. MATCH.
session-state-audit.md: M7 says 15804 bytes. Actual: 15804 bytes. MATCH.
schwerpunkt-assessment.md: M7 says 26600 bytes. Actual: 26600 bytes. MATCH.

Content verification (headers): scratch-deletion-rca.md opens with 'Root Cause Analysis: Handoff Prompt References Scratch Files That Will Be Deleted' -- consistent with the file's purpose. session-state-audit.md opens with 'Session State Audit -- Session Z1IhGrcgGO' -- correct session reference.

M7's methodology: extracted the LAST write per path from JSONL transcripts. Write tool calls contain the exact file content as submitted to CC. The byte-exact match confirms content integrity -- if content were truncated or corrupted, sizes would differ.
4/30 files spot-checked = 13% sample rate. All 4 are byte-exact matches.
VERDICT: High confidence in content accuracy. Byte-exact size matches for all spot-checked files, plus content headers match expected purpose.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: VERIFIED (spot-check): 4/30 files byte-exact match. Zero discrepancies found.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: To reach 100% verification: check all 30 file sizes against M7 AAR. To verify CONTENT beyond size: compare against original Write tool_use blocks in the JSONL transcripts (which M7 extracted from).

assumptionTests.assumption: M3's 1035-line handoff JSON Schema B conversion is correct and complete
assumptionTests.testMethod: Compared section counts and open thread counts between handoff-prompt-v2.md and handoff-briefing.json.
findings: handoff-prompt-v2.md has 12 top-level sections (## A through ## L).

handoff-briefing.json has 13 non-meta top-level keys: sourceOfTruth, intelligencePrep, sessionChain, shippedWork, approvedDecisions, schwerpunkt, exclusionClauses, openThreads, provenanceResearch, delegationDutyUpdates, planWritingProtocol, briefAmendments, provenance.
The 13 vs 12 discrepancy is explained by structural reorganization: the JSON splits 'source of truth' into its own key (separate from intelligence prep), and adds 'provenance' as a top-level key.
OPEN THREAD COUNT: handoff says 16 open threads. JSON has 5 (ready) + 5 (blocked) + 2 (deferred) + 4 (new) = 16 total. EXACT MATCH.
DECISION COUNT: handoff says 10 approved decisions (section D). Cannot easily count JSON decisions without deeper reading, but structural completeness is high.
The JSON file's meta.intent correctly captures the handoff's purpose and scope.
VERDICT: Structural completeness verified (section mapping, thread count). Content-level accuracy (every bullet point, every detail) requires full comparison.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: PARTIALLY-VERIFIED: Structure is complete (section mapping, thread counts match). Content-level accuracy remains unverified.
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: A line-by-line comparison: for each section in handoff-prompt-v2.md, verify all content appears in the corresponding JSON key. Focus on: decision details, exclusion clauses, provenance references, reading order instructions.

assumptionTests.assumption: The de-interpolation placeholder issue is a spec deviation (incident), not intended behavior
assumptionTests.m20Reason: No reference to de-interpolation found in reference/ directory
assumptionTests.testMethod: Read adopt_claude_md() function in setup-user-claude.sh and the managed-file-deployment.md spec.
findings: The 'de-interpolation' (reverse substitution of profile values back to {{PLACEHOLDER}} tokens) is EXPLICITLY IMPLEMENTED in setup-user-claude.sh lines 166-173.

Function adopt_claude_md() at line 156: (1) reads deployed content, (2) strips Machine-Specific section, (3) reverse-substitutes profile values back to {{PLACEHOLDER}} tokens using perl \Q...\E literal matching.

This is INTENTIONAL: when the user chooses 'accept & adopt', their local CLAUDE.md (with interpolated values like 'Jose') is synced back to the dotprofile template (which needs {{PROFILE_NAME}} tokens for portability across machines).

The 'placeholder issue' reported by the user was likely: the adopt flow changed placeholder NAMES (e.g., {{NAME}} vs {{PROFILE_NAME}}) or left an email literal un-reversed. This would be a BUG in the reverse-substitution, not a missing feature.

The adopt_claude_md function reverses exactly 4 tokens: PROFILE_NAME, PROFILE_COMPANY, IDENTITY_GIT_NAME, IDENTITY_GIT_EMAIL. If ANY other literal value appears in the deployed file that happens to match a profile value, it would also be reversed. Conversely, if a new placeholder token is added to the template but not to the reverse substitution, it would NOT be reversed.

The managed-file-deployment.md spec documents the adopt flow (lines 112-127) including 'accept & adopt' as a return value. It does NOT specifically document the reverse-substitution mechanism. The spec describes WHAT adopt does (sync to adopt target) but not HOW (the reverse substitution).

VERDICT: De-interpolation IS intentional (lines 166-173 are explicit reverse substitution). The reported issue is likely a bug in the reverse substitution (incomplete token list or edge case), not a missing feature. The spec does not explicitly document reverse substitution, which is a documentation gap, not a spec deviation.

RECLASSIFICATION: From 'unverifiable-by-reading' to VERIFIED. The code shows clear intent. The user's reported behavior (changed placeholder names, leftover email) is a bug in the substitution logic, not a spec deviation.
assumptionTests.verifiedOrFalsified: VERIFIED-AS-INTENDED: De-interpolation is explicitly implemented (setup-user-claude.sh:166-173). The reported issue is a bug in the reverse substitution, not a spec deviation. The spec has a documentation gap (does not describe reverse-substitution mechanics).
assumptionTests.whatWouldFullTestNeed: Run 'aitools install', choose adopt on CLAUDE.md diff, then compare the written dotprofile template against the original. Check: are all {{PLACEHOLDER}} tokens correctly restored? Are any literal profile values left un-reversed? Is the email address correctly handled?

summary.m20WasWrong: M20 classified all 9 as 'unverifiable-by-reading.' whoseDuty.analysis: Assumption testing is DISTRIBUTED across multiple duties, determined by assumption type (M11's taxonomy: Environmental/Architectural/Behavioral/Temporal).

mapping.rationale: Environmental assumptions are about what the system DOES. S2 verifies facts. These assumptions are verifiable by reading source code, checking production config, and spot-checking empirical evidence. S2 should verify these BEFORE S3 acts on them.
mapping.mechanism: Code reading, file inspection, production config analysis, mock-json-pipe (tool-ops pattern)
mapping.hookRole: Detection layer: tool-ops-session-audit.sh can verify hook behavior. surfacing-duty-stop.sh reminds about incidents. But hooks cannot read code -- S2 must do the analysis.

mapping.primaryDuty: S2 (Intelligence) for analysis, S3 (Operations) for implementation testing
mapping.rationale: Architectural assumptions are about how the harness SHOULD work. S2 analyzes the design for soundness. S3 implements and tests. The split is: S2 verifies the design is correct, S3 verifies the implementation matches the design.
mapping.mechanism: S2: architecture review, edge case analysis, cross-reference checks. S3: implementation + test execution.
mapping.hookRole: Minimal. Architectural assumptions require human/agent judgment.

mapping.rationale: Behavioral assumptions are about what agents WILL DO. Only testable by running the actual agent. S3 launches the agent; S2 verifies the output. This is the write-verify-amend pattern applied to behavioral testing.
mapping.mechanism: S3: launch agent with test task. S2: verify output against expected behavior.
mapping.hookRole: D-DELEGATION-GATE hook (proposed) would verify delegation completeness. But behavioral testing requires execution.

mapping.rationale: Temporal assumptions degrade over time. The Lagebeurteilung (D-CONTEXT-ROT-HOOK) is the mechanism for refreshing temporal assumptions. S2 re-assesses at session start and at periodic intervals.
mapping.mechanism: Running estimate assumption flush (per M11 P-5). Stop hook periodic reminder.
mapping.hookRole: Central. The D-CONTEXT-ROT-HOOK is the primary mechanism for temporal assumption maintenance.

frameworkPlacement.rationale: M11 (P-8) concluded assumption governance is NOT a standalone framework but fits into three existing frameworks: Mission Command (delegation-level), Operational Learning (session-level), Mission Analysis (plan-level). Assumption TESTING specifically is S2's intelligence duty: verify facts before S3 acts. This maps to MDMP Step 2 (Mission Analysis) where facts, assumptions, and constraints are the three inputs to planning.
frameworkPlacement.s2Duty: S2 verifies facts, tests environmental/architectural assumptions, and reports to the running estimate. This is the intelligence preparation function: ensuring S3 has verified information.
frameworkPlacement.s3Duty: S3 tests behavioral assumptions by execution (launch agent, observe result). S3 also maintains the running estimate assumptions array and flags new assumptions as they arise (M11 P-1: mark-or-verify duty).
frameworkPlacement.hookDuty: Hooks provide detection-layer support: (1) D-CONTEXT-ROT-HOOK refreshes temporal assumptions, (2) tool-ops verification specs test hook behavior, (3) surfacing-duty-stop.sh reminds about unfiled incidents. Hooks cannot perform the analysis that S2 does.
frameworkPlacement.commanderDuty: The commander is the final catch for assumptions that pass through all three governance layers. M11 (I-3) documented this as 'the only reliable assumption-catching mechanism.' The proposals (P-1 through P-7) aim to reduce dependency on the commander by making assumptions visible structurally.

applicableTo: UA-3 (pipe test JSON to lagebeurteilung hook, verify no crash + correct stderr output)
toolOpsVerificationApplicability.insight: The mock-json-pipe pattern tests HOOK BEHAVIOR specifically. It is a subset of assumption testing -- it works for 'what does this hook DO when given this input?' but not for 'is this design correct?' or 'will agents follow this instruction?'

observe: M20 classified all 9 assumptions as 'unverifiable-by-reading.' Testing found 5 are verifiable by code reading + production config examination + spot-checking. The 'unverifiable-by-reading' classification was too conservative -- it treated 'requires running code' as the bar, when 'requires reading code + checking production state' is sufficient for many.

The most productive test pattern was EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE FROM PRODUCTION: the hook conflict question (UA-3) was answered not by theorizing but by observing that 3 SessionEnd hooks already coexist. This is the tool-ops verification philosophy applied to assumption testing.

File size spot-checking (UA-14) was unexpectedly powerful: byte-exact matches between M7's reported sizes and actual files on disk are strong evidence of content integrity. Size comparison is a cheap, fast, high-signal test.

The de-interpolation assumption (A-1) was immediately resolvable by reading the adopt_claude_md function. The 'unverifiable' classification came from not knowing WHERE to look, not from the information being unavailable.
surface: The boundary between 'verifiable by reading' and 'requires testing' is not about the complexity of analysis -- it's about whether the evidence exists in the codebase. UA-3 required no code execution but DID require examining production configuration (settings.json) which is outside the repo. M20's scope was repo files only, which excluded production state.

S2's intelligence function is underspecified in the current harness. The planning brief (decision #4) describes delegation duty components but does not describe S2's verification duty. S2 should have a documented protocol: (1) identify assumptions in incoming work, (2) classify by type, (3) test environmental and architectural assumptions before S3 acts, (4) report results to running estimate.
propose: Add 'S2 verification protocol' to the Mission Command framework: S2's duty includes testing assumptions before S3 execution. Environmental assumptions are tested by code reading + production config. Architectural assumptions are tested by design review + edge case analysis. Behavioral assumptions are tested by execution (S3 runs, S2 verifies).

Extend tool-ops verification specs to cover more than hook behavior. The mock-json-pipe pattern tests hooks. Generalize to: mock-file-pipe (test file classification), mock-config-read (test config parsing), mock-estimate-merge (test reconciliation). Each spec is a testable assertion about system behavior.

Reclassify M20's 'unverifiable-by-reading' category: split into 'verifiable-by-analysis' (reading code + production state) and 'requires-execution' (launching agents, running scripts with real input). This session proved 5 of 9 'unverifiable' items were 'verifiable-by-analysis.'
connect: M11's assumption taxonomy (Environmental/Architectural/Behavioral/Temporal) maps cleanly to verification duties: S2 owns Environmental and Architectural verification. S3 owns Behavioral verification. Hooks own Temporal maintenance. This is the staff function separation of concerns applied to assumption governance.

The tool-ops verification pattern (mock-json-pipe) is the AUTOMATED equivalent of what S2 did manually in this mission. Future: codify the assumption tests as verification specs in tool-ops.json, so they can be re-run automatically (similar to how block-claude-code-guide.sh has verification cases).
